title: The King Who Is Our Peace
introduction:
Before You Begin

These commentaries grow out of this week’s passage. They are not required, and they are not the main thing. They are simply here to help, a little extra for your study. Feel free to use them or not, and to choose the point that best fits your group’s conversation. You do not need to cover everything. What matters most is to read the passage, pray, study it together and let it reach your hearts, so that we respond to God in obedience to his Word. Each point also opens other themes you can explore, as your time and energy allow. Our prayer is that God will guide you, give you wisdom and bring fruit from your time in his Word.

Only the Bible is inspired by God. These commentaries are human reflections, always read them under the authority of God’s Word.

In 2 Samuel 7, God promised David a throne that would last forever. In Isaiah 9, he promised a child who would sit on that throne. Now Micah, who lived in the same years as Isaiah, tells us where this King will come from, what he will bring and how he will lead. These three reflections follow the passage: a small town and an eternal King, a peace that is a person, and a Shepherd who never uses his sheep.

points.title: A Small Town and an Eternal King
points.text:
Micah 5 opens with a dark picture. The city is under attack, and “they will strike the judge of Israel with a rod on the cheek” (Micah 5:1). Then, suddenly, God speaks to a tiny village: “But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, being small among the clans of Judah, out of you one will come out to me who is to be ruler in Israel” (Micah 5:2).

Bethlehem was never an important place. In David’s time, the Philistines once kept soldiers there (2 Samuel 23:14), and later King Rehoboam built defenses around it (2 Chronicles 11:6). But it never grew into a great city. It was known mainly as David’s hometown, “the village where David was” (John 7:42).

Centuries later, David’s family had fallen very low. Joseph and Mary came from the line of kings, but they traveled to Bethlehem as ordinary, poor people. There was no room for them, and the baby was laid “in a feeding trough” (Luke 2:7). When they presented him at the temple, they offered two birds, the offering God allowed for families who could not afford a lamb (Luke 2:24, Leviticus 12:8).

Yet Micah says something amazing about this ruler: his “goings out are from of old, from ancient times.” His story did not begin in Bethlehem. Christians hear in these words a hint of his eternal origin. John says, “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1), and Jesus said, “Before Abraham came into existence, I AM” (John 8:58).

So Bethlehem cannot explain Jesus. Things produce after their own kind, and a feeding trough does not produce a Messiah. Sometimes great people do rise from humble places, but Jesus’ greatness did not come from his background. It came from God. Last week we saw that God often begins his work in what looks small. This week adds something more. Our background does not decide our value to God. His call does.

Reflection question

Jesus’ greatness did not come from where he was born, but from God. How can this truth encourage us when we feel that where we come from, or what we lack, limits what God can do through us?

Optional Ideas to Explore

- Matthew 2:4 to 6 · Knowing the address, missing the King. When the wise men asked where the King would be born, the religious leaders answered at once, “In Bethlehem of Judea,” quoting Micah. They knew the right verse, but they did not go. Knowing the Bible well is a gift, but it is not the same as coming to Jesus.

- 1 Corinthians 1:27 to 29 · God chooses what the world overlooks. “God chose the weak things of the world that he might put to shame the things that are strong ... that no flesh should boast before God.” God’s way of choosing people and places leaves no room for pride, and a lot of room for hope.

points.title: A Peace That Is a Person
points.text:
Micah says of this King, “He will be our peace when Assyria invades our land” (Micah 5:5). Notice something important. Peace here is not only a situation. It is a person. The King himself will be their peace.

And notice when he is their peace. Not after every danger is gone, but “when Assyria invades.” Our reading stops here, but the next verses show that the Assyrian threat was still on the horizon (Micah 5:6). God’s peace does not always remove the threat. It gives us a King who stands with us inside it.

Christians can see two kinds of peace here. The first is peace with God. Our sin had made us his enemies, but in Christ “we have peace with God” (Romans 5:1). Paul says, “he is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14). Paul is speaking about a different situation than Micah, but the heart is the same: peace has a name. The second is peace before the future. For Israel the threat was Assyria. For us it can be many things: illness, money, a job, papers, the future of our family.

There is a paradox here. Many wars in history have been driven by leaders and fed by ego, ambition and the desire for control. Those leaders send their people to fight and die for them. Jesus, our King and Shepherd, does the opposite. He gives his own life for his people. He made “peace through the blood of his cross” (Colossians 1:20).

Just before our passage, Micah speaks of the “tower of the flock” (Micah 4:8), a place near Bethlehem already named in Genesis (Genesis 35:19 to 21). Some Bible teachers, based on old Jewish writings, believe that the shepherds near Bethlehem cared for animals that would later be offered as sacrifices in the temple. We cannot be certain, but if so, it is beautiful. The first people to hear the angels sing “on earth peace” (Luke 2:14) were men watching over lambs for sacrifice. And the baby they went to see would one day be called “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29).

Reflection question

Jesus does not only promise to calm our circumstances. He himself is our peace, even when the threats are still there. How can knowing him in this way change how we face our fears about the future?

Optional Ideas to Explore

- Isaiah 53:7 · The Lamb who did not fight back. “As a lamb that is led to the slaughter ... so he didn’t open his mouth.” The King who brings peace did it by giving himself, not by sending others to suffer for him.

- Philippians 4:6 to 7 · Peace that guards the heart. “In nothing be anxious ... And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.” This peace does not depend on understanding everything that is coming. It depends on the One who guards us.

points.title: A Shepherd Who Never Uses His Sheep
points.text:
“He shall stand, and shall shepherd in the strength of Yahweh, in the majesty of the name of Yahweh his God. They will live” (Micah 5:4). This King leads like a shepherd. He stands firm, and his people can live in safety.

To see why this matters, look back at Micah 3. There, God accuses the leaders of his people with terrible words. They “eat the flesh of my people” and “break their bones” (Micah 3:2 to 3). They used the people instead of caring for them. The promised King is the opposite. Protecting, feeding and gathering the flock are not extras. They are part of what real authority is. As we saw in week 1, God pictures his King as a shepherd.

Micah also says this Shepherd leads “in the majesty of the name of Yahweh.” In the Bible, God’s name is not just a label. It speaks of who God is, his reputation, his authority and his presence with his people. So this King is not a hero acting on his own, and his right to rule does not come only from being in David’s family. He represents God.

This is important because Micah’s leaders also used God’s name. They lived with bribes and injustice, and still they said, “Isn’t Yahweh among us? No disaster will come on us” (Micah 3:11). They used God’s presence like an automatic guarantee. Micah 5 does not support that. God’s name does not approve every leader who speaks about God. It stands behind the shepherd who feeds, gathers and protects. So we avoid two mistakes. We do not reduce leadership to political skill, and we do not treat as holy every leader who uses God’s name.

Jesus is this Shepherd. He told his Father, “I revealed your name to the people whom you have given me” (John 17:6). And he said, “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11).

Reflection question

Jesus is the Shepherd who leads us without ever using us. How can resting in his care shape the way we lead and serve others, at home, at work or in the church?

Optional Ideas to Explore

- Ezekiel 34:15 to 16 · God himself as Shepherd. After rejecting the shepherds who fed themselves, God says, “I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep ... I will seek that which was lost ... and will bind up that which was broken.” This is the heart of the Shepherd that Micah promised.

- 1 Peter 5:2 to 4 · Leading under the Chief Shepherd. “Shepherd the flock of God which is among you ... not as lording it over those entrusted to you, but making yourselves examples to the flock.” Every leader in the church serves under “the chief Shepherd,” and leads best by following him.
